body.fr:
English nouns have no gender, which simplifies things — but articles still follow clear rules.

ArticleUsageExample
aindefinite, before a consonant sounda book
anindefinite, before a vowel soundan apple
thedefinite, a specific thingthe book on the table
(none)general/plural/uncountableI like music
The choice between a and an depends on the sound, not the letter: an hour (silent h) but a university (sounds like "y").

RuleExample
+ s (most nouns)cat → cats
+ es (after s, x, ch, sh, z)box → boxes
y → ies (consonant + y)city → cities
f/fe → vesleaf → leaves
irregularman → men, child → children, mouse → mice

SubjectObjectFrançais
Imeje / moi
youyoutu / toi
hehimil / lui
sheherelle
ititil/elle (chose)
weusnous
theythemils/elles
Unlike French, the subject pronoun is never dropped in English: you must always say I speak, never just speak.

English distinguishes habits/facts from actions happening right now.

Present simplePresent continuous
formI work / he worksI am working
usehabits, facts, routinesactions in progress, temporary situations
exampleI work every day.I am working right now.
Remember the -s at the third person singular in the simple present: he works, she plays, it rains — a very common mistake for French speakers to forget.

title.fr: The verbs to be and to have

body.fr:
Pronounto beto have
Iamhave
youarehave
he/she/itishas
wearehave
you (pl.)arehave
theyarehave
I am tired and I have a headache.
Je suis fatigué et j'ai mal à la tête.

Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs must be learned by heart.

TypeExample
regularwork → worked
irregulargo → went, see → saw, have → had
Yesterday I went to the market and bought some bread.
Hier je suis allé au marché et j'ai acheté du pain.
Questions and negatives in the past use the auxiliary did + base form: Did you go? / I didn't go (not I didn't went).

This tense has no direct equivalent in French usage — it links the past to the present.

I have lived in Marseille for ten years.
Je vis à Marseille depuis dix ans (et j'y vis toujours).
Use the present perfect for an action that started in the past and continues now (with for/since), or for a past action with a present result — not for a finished, dated event (which takes the past simple: I visited Rome in 2019).

FormUseExample
will + baseprediction, decision made nowIt will rain tomorrow.
going to + baseplan, intention already decidedI am going to study tonight.
present continuousfixed arrangementI am meeting her at 5pm.

Most negatives are built with the auxiliary do/does/did + not + base verb (except with be and modal verbs).

I don't like coffee. She doesn't speak German.
Je n'aime pas le café. Elle ne parle pas allemand.
Unlike Spanish or French, English never uses a double negative: say I don't have anything, not I don't have nothing.

Most questions require inversion with an auxiliary (do/does/did, or be, or a modal).

Where do you live? / Are you tired? / Can you help me?
Où habites-tu ? / Es-tu fatigué ? / Peux-tu m'aider ?

For possession between people, English often uses 's: Anna's book (le livre d'Anna) — the possessor comes first, unlike French.

readings.title: My family
readings.t: My name is Anna. I am twenty years old and I study at university. My family is small: my father, my mother and my brother. My father works at a bank and my mother is a teacher. My brother's name is Paul and he is fifteen years old. We live in a house near the city center. On Sundays we all eat together at my grandparents' house.

readings.title: A normal day
readings.t: Every day I get up at seven in the morning. I have bread and coffee for breakfast and I leave the house at eight. I go to class by bus. Classes finish at five in the afternoon. Afterwards, I go to the gym or meet my friends. In the evening, I have dinner with my family and watch a bit of television before sleeping.

readings.title: A trip to London
readings.t: Last year I travelled to London with two friends. We arrived by plane and went straight to the hotel. For three days we visited the Tower of London, Camden Market and the Thames. We ate fish and chips in many small restaurants and practised our English with local people. On the last day we bought gifts for our families before returning to France. It was an unforgettable trip.

readings.title: My summer job
readings.t: This summer I worked in a coffee shop in the city center. I started at nine in the morning and finished at four in the afternoon. At first it was difficult because I spoke little English, but over time I understood the customers better. My coworkers were very friendly and helped me a lot. I learned to make coffee and to talk with people. It was a very useful experience to improve my English.

readings.t: Artificial intelligence is already part of our everyday life, even if we are not always aware of it. Virtual assistants, the recommendation systems of streaming platforms and spell checkers are just a few examples. On the one hand, it automates repetitive tasks and frees up time for more creative activities; on the other hand, some jobs are at risk of disappearing. readings.title: The rise of responsible consumption
readings.t: In recent decades, a growing awareness has emerged around the environmental impact of consumption. More and more consumers, when buying, take into account not only the price, but also the ecological footprint of the product, the working conditions of those who make it and the durability of the item in question. This paradigm shift has forced many companies to rethink their production processes and adopt more transparent practices. However, some critics warn that this phenomenon risks becoming a mere marketing strategy —known as 'greenwashing'— if it is not accompanied by real and verifiable commitments.

readings.title: Collective memory and the construction of identity
readings.t: Collective memory plays a fundamental role in the construction of a society's identity, insofar as it shapes the way a human group interprets its own past. Far from being a mere accumulation of historical facts, this memory is constantly built and rebuilt according to the interests, tensions and sensitivities of the present. Hence certain historical episodes become the subject of periodic, often controversial, reinterpretations, which reflect both advances in historical knowledge and the ideological transformations of each era. In this sense, one might ask to what extent it is possible —or even desirable— to aspire to a single, unequivocal collective memory, given that the plurality of perspectives ultimately constitutes one of the pillars of any democratic society.
